Specimen Collection

Collecting blood, urine, sputum, stool and wound swabs correctly for culture and testing.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe correct collection of blood, urine, sputum, stool and wound swabs
  • State how to prevent contamination
  • Explain labelling and transport of specimens

In simple words

Specimen collection is obtaining body fluids or tissues for laboratory testing and culture. Correct collection is vital — a contaminated or wrongly labelled specimen gives wrong results and wrong treatment.

The nurse collects, labels, transports and documents the specimen.

Collection methods

Specimen Method Key point
Blood Venipuncture into correct tube Aseptic technique; correct tube
Urine Midstream clean-catch Clean genital area first; midstream
Sputum Deep cough into sterile container Not saliva; early morning best
Stool Clean container; no urine/water Collect from different areas
Wound swab Swab the wound bed, not the edge Clean wound first if possible

Preventing contamination

  • Clean the site before collecting.
  • Do not touch the inside of the container or the swab tip.
  • Collect before antibiotics when possible.
  • Transport promptly to the lab.

Labelling and transport

Label with: patient name, ID number, date/time, specimen type, test requested. Send to lab quickly — some specimens (blood cultures, blood gases) are time-critical.

🔴 Right specimen, right result

A contaminated or wrongly labelled specimen gives wrong results and wrong treatment. Collect carefully, label clearly, send promptly.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Blood culture — collect before antibiotics; use aseptic technique; correct blood culture bottles.
  • Midstream urine — clean the genital area; discard first stream; collect midstream.
  • Sputum — instruct patient to cough deeply from the chest, not spit saliva; collect early morning.
  • Wound swab — swab the wound bed (pus/tissue), not the edge or dry crust.
  • Labelling — two identifiers; date and time; send to lab without delay.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Specimen collection obtains body fluids/tissues for testing and culture.
  2. Blood: aseptic venipuncture into correct tube (before antibiotics for cultures).
  3. Urine: midstream clean-catch after cleaning the genital area.
  4. Sputum: deep cough from chest into sterile container (not saliva).
  5. Wound swab: swab the wound bed, not the edge.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Label with name, ID, date/time, specimen type and test requested.
  2. Transport promptly — time-critical specimens (blood cultures, blood gases).
  3. Do not touch inside of container or swab tip.
  4. Document collection in the patient record.

📌 Memory trick

Specimen labels: “N-I-D-T-T” — Name, ID, Date/Time, Type of specimen, Test.

60-second revision

  • Specimen = body fluid/tissue for testing.
  • Blood: aseptic, correct tube, before antibiotics.
  • Urine: midstream clean-catch.
  • Sputum: deep cough, not saliva, early morning.
  • Wound swab: wound bed, not edge.
  • Label: name, ID, date/time, type, test; send promptly.

Test yourself

A midstream urine specimen means:

Answer: B. Midstream clean-catch: discard the first part of the stream, then collect the middle portion.

Sputum is:

Answer: B. Sputum is material coughed up from the lungs and airways, not saliva from the mouth.

Blood culture should be collected:

Answer: B. Blood cultures are collected before antibiotics so the organism is not killed by the drug.

A wound swab should be taken from:

Answer: B. Swab the wound bed (where pus/tissue is) to get the infecting organism.

Specimens should be labelled with:

Answer: B. Label with name, ID number, date/time, specimen type and test requested.
